The Watases lanternfish (Diaphus watasei) attains a maximum recorded standard length of 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-sized members of its genus in the western Pacific. This ultimate length is achieved following a protracted growth phase that reflects the cold, mesopelagic environment the species inhabits. At the onset of reproductive capability, individuals measure approximately 10.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10.1 centimeters] in standard length, a value derived from comparisons with the closely related congener Diaphus dumerilii and which marks the transition from the sub-adult to the mature phase. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal stage is estimated at 8.2 grams [Wwp = 8.2 grams], a relatively modest mass that underscores the energetic constraints imposed by the deep-sea habitat. These morphometric benchmarks were established from extensive trawl surveys conducted throughout the species' known range off the coasts of Japan and Taiwan, where adult specimens regularly approach the upper size limit, though the largest individuals remain comparatively rare in collections.

Under the prevailing thermal conditions of its deep-sea environment, which average 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], the reproductive biology of Diaphus watasei exhibits a remarkably high output. At this stable temperature, females can achieve a maximum daily reproductive rate, which in practical terms translates into a substantial spawning effort over the course of a breeding season. The species produces a clutch of approximately 39.5 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 39.5 eggs per spawning event], and spawning occurs multiple times daily, with females participating in roughly 850 spawning events each year [F_R_i = roughly 850 spawning events each year]. This extraordinary combination of moderate clutch size and extremely high spawning frequency results in a prodigious annual fecundity that is well suited to offset the high mortality rates typical of pelagic larval stages in the oligotrophic waters of the mesopelagic zone. Such a reproductive strategy is consistent with that observed in other myctophids that inhabit similarly cold, food-limited environments.

The early life history of Diaphus watasei begins with a minute hatchling, as the fertilized eggs, which are pelagic and transparent, give rise to yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams] at the moment of eclosion. This exceptionally low neonatal wet weight is a consequence of the small egg diameter, approximately 0.5 millimeters, and reflects the species' strategy of producing numerous, minimally provisioned offspring. During the subsequent lecithotrophic phase, these protolarvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves while suspended in the water column at depths where the ambient temperature remains near 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. The yolk-sac stage lasts until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the larvae must successfully capture their first prey—typically copepod nauplii—to avoid the point of no return. This critical transition represents a major bottleneck in the species' population dynamics, as larval survival is heavily contingent upon the seasonal availability of suitable zooplankton prey in the surrounding waters.

As females reach their full somatic growth potential, the ultimate wet weight attained by mature individuals is approximately 39.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 39.5 grams], a body mass that is achieved after several years of continuous feeding in the mesopelagic zone. This asymptotic mass, derived from length-weight relationships fitted to field-collected specimens, represents the upper bound of somatic investment before resources are fully diverted into the prodigious reproductive effort described earlier. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty of 8.2 grams [Wwp = 8.2 grams] indicates that maturation occurs at a relatively small fraction—roughly one-fifth—of the ultimate adult mass, a pattern that is common among myctophids and other deep-sea teleosts that face high mortality risks and therefore benefit from early reproduction. The allometric relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical cubic function, and the body condition of adult females remains robust throughout the year, supported by a diet dominated by copepods and small euphausiids.

Longevity records for Diaphus watasei indicate that the maximum lifespan, under the stable thermal regime of its mesopelagic habitat at 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], reaches approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This lifespan is consistent with the relatively fast-paced life history observed in many myctophid species, where early maturity and high reproductive output are balanced against a moderate maximum age. The longest-lived individuals are typically those that occupy the lower portion of the species' depth range, where predation pressure from visually orienting predators is reduced and food availability remains more consistent throughout the year. Senescence in this species is likely accompanied by a gradual decline in fecundity and body condition during the final year of life, though direct observations of senescent individuals in the wild remain scarce. The interplay between the 5-year maximum lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] and the species' high daily reproductive rate underscores a life history strategy finely tuned to the challenges of a cold, dark, and resource-patchy environment at a temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C].
